captions: July twenty-first — a huge earnings day.
Around forty-five companies reported their first-quarter results.
Whose profit jumped, whose fell,
and what's the story behind each number —
let's break it all down.
One key point —
all these results are compared with the same quarter last year,
that is, year-on-year.
This is information analysis only — not investment advice.
First, today's top three profits.
Number one — Bajaj Auto.
Net profit of three thousand two hundred twenty-six crore —
up forty-six percent from last year.
Number two — TVS Motor.
Profit of one thousand fifty-eight crore —
up sixty-five percent.
This is the highest quarterly profit in the company's history.
Number three — Mahindra and Mahindra Financial.
Profit of nine hundred twenty-seven crore —
surging seventy-five percent.
Autos and financials led today.
But there's an important reason behind Bajaj Auto's number —
we'll look at it shortly.
Now the four strong results in detail.
First — Bajaj Auto.
Net profit three thousand two hundred twenty-six crore,
revenue twenty-one thousand six hundred eighty-nine crore —
up sixty-five percent.
But this big jump came from a consolidation change —
more on that soon.
Second — TVS Motor.
Profit one thousand fifty-eight crore,
up sixty-five percent — an all-time Q1 high.
Electric vehicle sales rose eighty-six percent.
After the results, the stock jumped six percent.
Third — M&M Financial.
Profit nine hundred twenty-seven crore,
up seventy-five percent.
Disbursements rose twenty-one percent and assets twelve percent.
Fourth — Bandhan Bank.
Profit five hundred two crore, up thirty-five percent —
driven by lower provisions and better asset quality.
Its net interest margin was six point two percent.
Many more companies reported too.
Let's look at four important ones.
First — Sagility, a healthcare BPO company.
Revenue two thousand twenty-four crore,
up nearly twenty-eight percent.
Profit rose seventy-three point five percent.
Second — NIIT.
Revenue rose fourteen percent,
but profit surged eighty-five percent,
driven by skilling and training demand.
Third — IndiaMART, the B2B online marketplace.
Revenue four hundred fourteen crore,
profit one hundred seventy-two crore —
a steady twelve percent growth.
Fourth — Anthem Biosciences,
a recently listed pharma services company.
Profit one hundred twenty crore,
revenue four hundred eighteen crore.
Here's today's most important lesson —
numbers are never as simple as they look.
First myth — Bajaj Auto's revenue rose sixty-five percent,
so it's amazing.
No.
The company folded a foreign subsidiary into its accounts —
a consolidation change.
So the numbers can't be compared directly with last year.
The real organic growth is much lower.
Second myth — JSW Infrastructure's profit fell ten percent,
so it's a bad company.
No.
The profit fell because it diverted surplus cash to building new projects for future growth,
and paid more tax.
This isn't a demand problem — it's a deliberate investment.
Third myth — comparing with last quarter, that is QoQ,
is enough.
But most businesses have a seasonal effect — festivals,
summer.
So comparing with the same quarter last year, year-on-year,
is the correct analysis.
So how should you read any result?
Five rules.
One — look at four numbers: revenue, net profit, margin,
and management guidance.
Two — always compare with the same quarter last year,
that is year-on-year, not with the previous quarter.
Three —
check whether the headline percentage hides a one-time gain or a consolidation change —
like Bajaj Auto.
Four —
even a good result can fall short of market expectations,
and the stock may drop.
Five — one quarter isn't the whole story.
It's the trend and consistency over several quarters that really matter.
Today's results, at a glance.
The strong ones — TVS Motor up sixty-five percent,
M&M Financial seventy-five percent,
Bandhan Bank thirty-five percent.
Bajaj Auto rose forty-six percent —
but that was from a consolidation change.
More — Sagility seventy-three point five, NIIT eighty-five,
IndiaMART twelve percent.
The one that fell — JSW Infrastructure, down ten percent,
but because of capex.
The lesson — always look year-on-year,
and read the real story behind the headline percentage.
It's not the numbers —
it's the story behind them that is the real analysis.
This information is aggregated from public sources —
for analysis only, not investment advice.
Please consult an expert before making decisions.
Thanks for watching.
